items.question: 1/4 in vs 1/2 in router bit shank: which should a beginner buy?
items.short_answer: Start with 1/4 in (6.35 mm) shank. It fits any small or mid-size router. Move to 1/2 in only when your router is 2 HP or more and you cut deep profiles in hardwood.

items.question: How many router bits do you actually need? 6, 12 or 15 pieces?
items.short_answer: A 12-piece set is the practical sweet spot for most furniture and shelving work. Six is too few; fifteen mostly adds 1/2 in shank duplicates. Count profiles, not pieces.

items.question: What specs actually matter when buying a router bit set?
items.short_answer: Check four things: exact shank diameter (1/4 or 1/2 in), micro-grain carbide, sealed replaceable bearings, and how many distinct profiles the set contains. HRC numbers are marketing for wood cutting.

items.question: Carbide or high-speed steel: which router bits are worth the money?
items.short_answer: Buy carbide for anything used more than ten times; it lasts 10-25x longer than HSS in hardwood. HSS is only worth it for one-off softwood jobs.

items.question: 45, 55, 60, 65 degree router bits: what does the angle actually change?
items.short_answer: The angle describes cutting geometry: lower angles clear chips faster with more tear-out, higher angles give a cleaner finish in harder material at a slower feed. Ask sellers what the number refers to before comparing listings.

items.question: Cobalt or regular HSS drill bits for stainless steel?
items.short_answer: Use M35 cobalt (5% Co) with a 135 degree split point for stainless steel, at 300-500 rpm with constant pressure and cutting fluid. Regular HSS work-hardens stainless and dulls within a few holes.

items.question: Why does my diamond blade chip porcelain tile, and how do I stop it?
items.short_answer: Porcelain chips when you use a segmented blade at high rpm. Use a continuous-rim diamond blade at the low end of its rpm rating, wet if possible, and check the flange and 22.23 mm bore for wobble.

items.question: What grit sequence should I use when sanding wood?
items.short_answer: Double the grit roughly each step: 60, 120, 240, then 400 between finish coats. Each grit removes the previous grit's scratches; skipping steps wastes paper and leaves visible scratches.

items.question: Why is a $59 router bit set better than a $39 one?
items.short_answer: The difference is usually carbide grade, replaceable sealed bearings, shank tolerance and whether the advertised 12 profiles are actually 12 distinct shapes. A $39 set is rational for one softwood job; for MDF or oak used monthly, a dull bit burns the workpiece and the saving disappears.

items.question: 2, 3 or 4 flute end mill: which one for which material?
items.short_answer: 3-flute for aluminium, 4-flute for steel, 2-flute for plastics and deep slots. A 4-flute in aluminium clogs and welds; a 3-flute with polished or DLC flutes is the standard choice for non-ferrous work.

items.question: HRC55 or HRC65 end mills: is the harder grade worth it?
items.short_answer: HRC65 only pays off on hardened steel above about 45 HRC. On mild steel, stainless and aluminium, HRC55 is tougher, cheaper and finishes more parts before failing.

items.question: What is the actual difference between an aluminium end mill and a steel end mill?
items.short_answer: Aluminium end mills use 2-3 flutes, polished or DLC surfaces and a higher rake for chip clearance; steel end mills use 4 flutes, AlTiN coating and a stronger edge. Using one in the other material causes welding or rapid wear.

items.question: 3.175 mm, 6 mm or 8 mm shank: how do I pick?
items.short_answer: Match the collet: 3.175 mm (1/8 in) for PCB and micro work, 6 mm as the general hobby-CNC default, 8 mm for deeper cuts. 6 mm and 1/4 in are not interchangeable — they differ by 0.35 mm.

items.question: M35 or M42 cobalt drill bits: which for stainless steel?
items.short_answer: M35 (5% cobalt) covers most stainless work and is more forgiving; M42 (8%) only pays off in production on hard stainless with controlled speed. Cutting speed of 300-500 rpm matters more than the grade.

items.question: Masonry bit, hammer bit or regular drill bit: what is the difference?
items.short_answer: Masonry bits have a carbide tip for brick and block; SDS hammer bits have a reinforced shank for rotary hammers on concrete; HSS twist bits are for metal and wood only. Using a masonry bit on steel destroys the tip instantly.

items.question: Continuous, segmented or turbo rim diamond blade: which one?
items.short_answer: Continuous rim for chip-free porcelain and glazed tile, segmented for fast rough cuts in concrete and block, turbo as the compromise on hard stone. Glazed visible tile always gets continuous rim.

items.question: 24T, 40T or 60T saw blade: which tooth count for which job?
items.short_answer: 24T for fast ripping in softwood, 40T as the general crosscut blade, 60T+ for fine trim and veneered ply. A high tooth count in thick hardwood overheats because the gullets cannot clear chips.

items.question: Bi-metal or TCT hole saw: which one lasts?
items.short_answer: Bi-metal hole saws cut wood, plastics and thin sheet metal; TCT saws cut brick, block and fibre cement. Running a bi-metal saw in masonry with hammer action destroys it in one hole.

items.question: What rpm should I run a router bit at?
items.short_answer: Reduce rpm as bit diameter increases: up to 25 mm can run 18,000-24,000 rpm, 25-50 mm around 14,000-18,000, 50-75 mm about 10,000-14,000, and anything larger 8,000-12,000 or slower. Check the maximum rpm stamped on the shank.

items.question: Why does a Dyson V10 filter have a US version, and does it matter?
items.short_answer: The Dyson V10 has US, China/Japan and Slim (SV18) variants with different filter housings. Match the regional version before buying, then replace every 3-6 months.

items.question: How often should a Dyson pre-motor and post-motor filter be replaced?
items.short_answer: Wash the pre-motor filter monthly and replace it every 3-6 months. Replace the non-washable post-motor HEPA filter every 6-12 months. Loss of suction, musty smell or pulsing means it is overdue.

items.question: Do Dyson attachments fit every model, or does each model need its own tools?
items.short_answer: Plain Dyson tools fit V6-V15 and G5 interchangeably; powered heads, rollers and wands are model-specific. Buy plain tools generically, powered parts by exact model.

items.question: Is an 8 mm shank the same as 1/4 inch?
items.short_answer: No — 8 mm (0.315 in) and 1/4 in (6.35 mm) differ by 1.65 mm and need different collets.

items.question: Metric or imperial drill bits: does the difference matter?
items.short_answer: Yes. 6 mm and 1/4 in differ by 0.35 mm, enough to spoil a tapped hole or a press fit. Match the drawing's standard.

items.question: 118 or 135 degree drill point: which do I need?
items.short_answer: 118° for wood and mild steel, 135° split point for stainless and hard alloys. The split point stops the bit walking and work-hardening the surface.

items.question: What TPI hole saw do I need, and why do I need a separate arbor?
items.short_answer: 4/6 TPI variable pitch covers wood and sheet metal. The saw threads onto a specific arbor (1/2-20 or 5/8-18), so the pair must match.

items.question: What drill size do I use before tapping M3 to M12?
items.short_answer: Drill size = nominal diameter minus pitch: M3x0.5 → 2.5 mm, M6x1 → 5.0 mm, M10x1.5 → 8.5 mm, M12x1.75 → 10.2 mm.

items.question: NPT or BSP: how do I tell which thread a fitting is?
items.short_answer: NPT is 60° tapered (US), BSP is 55° (UK, EU, Asia). Half-inch sizes look nearly identical and will partially thread before leaking.

items.question: What does HRC mean on an end mill, and do I need the higher number?
items.short_answer: HRC describes the workpiece hardness the end mill is built for. HRC55 covers mild steel and stainless; HRC65 is for hardened steel and chips easily on light machines.

items.question: Up-cut, down-cut or compression router bit: which for plywood and veneer?
items.short_answer: Down-cut for a clean top surface, up-cut for chip clearance, compression for clean faces on both sides of plywood. Up-cut bits tear the visible top face.

items.question: Diamond blades come in 7/8 in and 20 mm bores — which fits my grinder?
items.short_answer: US angle grinders are usually 7/8 in (22.23 mm); many imported machines are 20 mm. Use a reducing ring rather than running a loose blade.

items.question: Carbide burr shapes: what do the letters A, C, D, E, F, G, H, L, M, N mean?
items.short_answer: The letters are head shapes: A cylinder, C ball, D ball-nose, E oval, F round-nose tree, G pointed tree, H flame, L taper, M cone, N inverted cone.

items.question: My router bits are burning the wood — replace the set or just the bit?
items.short_answer: Replace the set when more than two profiles burn, when the edge reflects light, or when you have to push harder than before. Cleaning a single bit often fixes a one-profile problem.

items.question: I snapped a drill bit mid-hole — what should I replace it with?
items.short_answer: Replace with an M35 cobalt bit for stainless or hard steel. Snapping usually means too much pressure or an already-dull bit, so fix the technique as well as the bit.

items.question: I broke a tap inside the hole — how do I get it out and what do I buy next?
items.short_answer: Use a tap extractor first; if it will not move, drill it out and fit a thread insert. Replace with an HSS or cobalt set for steel — carbon taps snap in steel.

items.question: My hole saw is cutting slowly — sharpen or replace?
items.short_answer: Bi-metal hole saws are not practically sharpenable. Replace the saw when the teeth are flattened or shiny; check the pilot bit and arbor first, since those fail more often.

items.question: How do I know a carbide burr is worn out, and what replaces it?
items.short_answer: Replace a burr when the flutes look polished, you need more pressure than before, or it smears instead of cutting. Keep the same shape code; single cut removes fast, double cut finishes smoother.

items.question: My router bit keeps slipping in the collet — what is wrong?
items.short_answer: Slipping means the wrong shank size, a worn collet, or a dirty bore. An 8 mm bit in a 1/4 in collet always slips — the sizes differ by 1.65 mm.

items.question: What router bit should I use for MDF?
items.short_answer: Use a 2-flute carbide straight bit for grooves and a bearing-guided round-over for edges. MDF is abrasive, so HSS dulls fast; carbide lasts far longer.

items.question: Why does melamine chip when I rout it and which bit stops it?
items.short_answer: Use a down-cut spiral to protect the top face, or a compression bit on 18 mm board to protect both faces. Scoring the line or taping it also stops chip-out.

items.question: How do I stop tear-out when routing plywood?
items.short_answer: Use a down-cut bit on the visible face, a backer board underneath, and a light climb cut on the last pass at the exit corner. Plywood tears out because each veneer layer runs a different direction.

items.question: How long does a router bit set actually last?
items.short_answer: Two to three years for a hobby shop, three to nine months for daily production. Heat and resin build-up end a bit's life long before the carbide wears out.

items.question: Are cheap router bit sets good enough?
items.short_answer: Cheap sets are fine in softwood for occasional use. They fail on hardwood and MDF because the carbide grade and bearings are where the cost was cut.

items.question: How should I store router bits so they do not rust or chip?
items.short_answer: Store bits upright in a wooden case with a silica pack, each in its own slot. Carbide chips against carbide, so bits must not rattle together.

items.question: Step drill or hole saw for sheet metal?
items.short_answer: Step drill for sheet metal under 4 mm and holes up to 35 mm. Hole saw for larger holes, thicker plate, wood and pipe.

items.question: Forstner bit or hole saw for a clean, flat-bottomed hole?
items.short_answer: Forstner for flat-bottomed holes, clean rims and controlled depth. Hole saw for through-holes, larger diameters, pipe and door locks.

items.question: Which arbor fits my hole saw?
items.short_answer: Match the arbor thread to the saw — 1/2-20 for most small saws, 5/8-18 for larger. Check the pilot drill size and the chuck capacity too.

items.question: Can a bi-metal hole saw cut stainless steel?
items.short_answer: Yes, but slowly: low rpm, constant cutting fluid, light pressure. Expect one to five holes in stainless rather than the dozens you get in mild steel.

items.question: Which drill bit actually works on stainless steel?
items.short_answer: Use M35 cobalt with a 135-degree split point, cutting fluid, and about a third of mild-steel rpm. Letting the bit rub instead of cut is what destroys stainless.

items.question: Best drill bit for hardwood?
items.short_answer: Brad-point for clean precise entry, auger for deep holes, Forstner for flat bottoms. Plain twist bits wander on hardwood.

items.question: How do you drill a hole in tile without cracking it?
items.short_answer: Carbide masonry bit at low rpm with hammer off, or a diamond hole saw with water. Hammer mode is what cracks tile.

items.question: How do I get out a stripped screw?
items.short_answer: Drill a pilot into the head, use a left-hand extractor turning counter-clockwise with steady pressure. Heat first if threadlocker was used.

items.question: Can a tap and die set repair stripped threads?
items.short_answer: Yes for burred threads — run the correct tap or die through to clean them. For torn-out threads you need a thread insert, since a tap cannot add material back.

items.question: How do I measure thread pitch without a gauge?
items.short_answer: Measure across ten threads with a caliper and divide by ten, or interlock threads with a known bolt. Pitch is crest-to-crest distance, not diameter.

items.question: Hand tap or machine tap?
items.short_answer: Hand taps are a three-piece set turned with a wrench. Machine taps cut in one pass and break if turned by hand. Use hand taps for repair, machine taps in a spindle.

items.question: Die stock or die wrench — which one do I need?
items.short_answer: Both hold the die and cut external threads; a die stock keeps the die squarer at the start, which is what determines whether the thread holds torque.

items.question: Which carbide burr for aluminium?
items.short_answer: Single cut, coarse tooth, run at roughly half steel rpm with wax lubricant. Aluminium welds onto a hot flute and then the burr stops cutting.

items.question: What rpm should I run a carbide burr at?
items.short_answer: Six mm head: about 25,000 rpm in aluminium, 14,000 in steel, 10,000 in stainless. Larger heads run proportionally slower.

items.question: What feed and speed should I use for CNC cutting wood?
items.short_answer: Rough starting point for a 6 mm bit: 18,000 rpm, 2,000-3,000 mm/min, 3 mm depth of cut, then adjust by chip size. Dust means too slow, burns mean the feed is too light.

items.question: Can I replace a worn bearing on a router bit?
items.short_answer: Yes. Measure the bore, outer diameter and width and fit a sealed bearing. A scored race means the bit was run without cleaning.

items.question: Do right-angle drill adapters work?
items.short_answer: For screws and small holes in tight spaces, yes. They cannot handle a hole saw or a large bit — the gears strip.

items.question: What size bits fit a 3/8 in chuck?
items.short_answer: A 3/8 in chuck takes round shanks up to 10 mm; a 1/2 in chuck up to 13 mm. Hex shanks up to 1/4 in fit both.

items.question: How do I get burnt resin off a router bit?
items.short_answer: Soak in oven cleaner or bit cleaner for 10-15 minutes and scrub with a brass brush. Never touch the carbide with a file or sandpaper.

items.question: Can you sharpen drill bits at home?
items.short_answer: Yes, on a bench grinder with an angle gauge for bits 3 mm and up. Hand-sharpened bits work in wood and mild steel but fail in stainless.

items.question: Why does my drill bit keep slipping in the chuck?
items.short_answer: The shank is not seated past the jaws, the shank is scored, or the jaws are worn. Seat it fully, tighten a keyed chuck in all three holes, and replace scored bits.

items.question: Keyless or keyed chuck — which holds better?
items.short_answer: A keyed chuck grips harder and stays tight under load. Keyless is faster for small bits but loosens with hole saws and large diameters.

items.question: How do I check whether my router or collet is out of true?
items.short_answer: Read a dial indicator on the bit shank below the collet: under 0.05 mm is healthy, over 0.1 mm means a bent shank or a worn collet.

items.question: Hex shank or round shank drill bits?
items.short_answer: Hex for impact drivers and quick-change holders, round for chucks and drill presses. Round shanks spin in an impact driver and hex shanks add runout in a press.

items.question: SDS Plus or SDS Max — which fits my rotary hammer?
items.short_answer: SDS Plus for rotary hammers up to about 1 in capacity, SDS Max for 1-1/2 in and above. The shanks are different sizes and do not interchange.

items.question: How do I drill a hole I cannot reach with a normal bit?
items.short_answer: Quick-change extensions for clearance holes, aircraft-length bits when accuracy matters. Any extension adds runout, so locate the hole with a short bit first.

items.question: How do you get a broken drill bit out of a hole?
items.short_answer: Grip and turn a proud bit back out; for a bit below the surface, drill a ring around it with a solid-carbide bit or have it spark-eroded. Never punch a hardened bit.

items.question: Can alum dissolve a broken tap?
items.short_answer: In aluminium, yes — a warm saturated alum solution dissolves the tap in one to three days. In steel it does nothing, so use spark erosion or an insert instead.

items.question: What is the best lubricant for tapping?
items.short_answer: Sulphurised tapping fluid for steel, kerosene or light oil for aluminium, dry for cast iron. In aluminium the wrong lubricant makes the chip weld to the flutes.

items.question: Is WD-40 good enough as cutting fluid?
items.short_answer: WD-40 works on aluminium and light drilling. On steel it evaporates too fast to protect the edge, so holes burn and work-harden.

items.question: What router bit do I need for oak and hickory?
items.short_answer: Carbide, 1/2 in shank above 6 mm depth, and 2-3 mm passes in hickory. These woods chip a 1/4 in shank on deep cuts.

items.question: Why does pine burn and fuzz when I route it?
items.short_answer: Pine burns because the bit dwells in the cut, not because rpm is too high. Keep a firm, continuous feed and stop at corners as little as possible.

items.question: How do you drill and cut ipe decking?
items.short_answer: Carbide cutters, a pilot hole for every screw, and wax on the blade. Ipe is dense and abrasive enough to destroy plain HSS bits in one deck.

items.question: TiN coated or black oxide drill bits?
items.short_answer: Black oxide for general work, TiN for repetitive steel drilling. The coating disappears at the first sharpening, so cobalt content matters more than colour.

items.question: AlTiN or TiAlN coating — does it matter?
items.short_answer: AlTiN and TiAlN are the same coating. It needs heat to work, so run it hard and dry in steel; in aluminium it fails because the chip welds to it.

items.question: Are diamond-coated router bits worth it?
items.short_answer: Only for carbon fiber and fiberglass, where they last far longer. On wood they add nothing, and a diamond-coated edge cannot be resharpened.

items.question: Jacobs taper or Morse taper for a drill chuck?
items.short_answer: Morse taper fits the machine spindle, Jacobs taper fits the chuck body. Read both numbers off the old arbor before ordering a replacement.

items.question: ER collet or R8 for a benchtop mill?
items.short_answer: R8 is the spindle interface, ER is the workholding. On an R8 mill you use an R8-to-ER adapter, so you need both.

items.question: What causes router kickback and how do I stop it?
items.short_answer: Kickback comes from feeding with the cutter rotation, too deep a pass, or a bit grabbing a corner. Feed against rotation and keep passes to 3 mm.

items.question: What should I check before using a router table?
items.short_answer: Check bit seating, fence locks, guard, featherboards and start-up clearance, with two push sticks in reach. Most table router injuries come from a check skipped, not a tool failure.

items.question: Do I need dust collection on a router table?
items.short_answer: Yes for MDF and production work. A shop vac at the fence port handles chips, and a box under the table catches the dust the cutter throws downward.

items.question: What am I actually paying for in a more expensive router bit set?
items.short_answer: Carbide grade, bearing quality and shank tolerance decide the price. A set that lists only piece count tells you nothing about how long it will cut.

items.question: Should I buy one good bit or a whole set?
items.short_answer: Buy one bit when you know the profile, a set when you are still exploring. Price per profile only wins if the single bit is the same carbide grade as the set.

items.question: Which tap and die set should I start with — metric or SAE?
items.short_answer: Buy metric if your fasteners are imported, SAE if they are US-built. NPT pipe threads come from neither set and need their own taps.

items.question: What size hole saw do I need for a door knob?
items.short_answer: A 2-1/8 in hole saw for the knob bore and 1 in for the latch. Drill the latch hole from the edge first, then bore the face from both sides.

items.question: What size auger bit should I use for running wire through studs?
items.short_answer: Three-quarter inch for one or two cables, 1 in if you may add more. Keep holes 1-1/4 in from the stud face or fit a nail plate.

items.question: What size hole saw for 1-1/2 in PVC pipe?
items.short_answer: For 1-1/2 in PVC, use a 2 in hole saw — the pipe is 1.900 in outside diameter, so nominal size and saw size never match.

items.question: How do I drill holes for fence posts?
items.short_answer: Use a power auger with a bit 2 in wider than the post and call 811 before digging. Pilot every rail hole 1 mm under the screw shank to stop splitting.

items.question: Do I need a 35 mm bit for concealed hinges?
items.short_answer: Yes — a 35 mm cup bore, 11-13 mm deep, 3-5 mm from the door edge. Use a Forstner with a depth stop, not a hole saw.

items.question: 8 degree or 14 degree dovetail bit?
items.short_answer: Eight degrees for through dovetails and drawers, 14 for half-blind joints and softwood. The bit angle must match the jig template, and they do not interchange.

items.question: How do I set router bit depth accurately?
items.short_answer: Set on scrap, cut, measure with a caliper and adjust in 0.1 mm steps. Router scales read from the base plate, so the measured cut is the only number that counts.

items.question: Should I climb cut with a router?
items.short_answer: Climb cut only as a 0.5 mm finishing pass with the work against a fence. Full-depth climb cuts pull the workpiece out of your hands.

items.question: Is one deep pass or several light passes faster?
items.short_answer: Light passes win overall: three at 3 mm cut faster than one at 9 mm once you count sanding and bit life. Keep depth under half the cutter diameter.

items.question: Why does my router burn the wood?
items.short_answer: Burn is friction: either the bit is dull or the feed is too slow for the rpm. Speed up the feed or drop 2,000 rpm, and clean resin off the flutes.

items.question: How do I rout a dado that actually holds a shelf?
items.short_answer: Measure the actual board thickness with calipers and cut a test dado first. Plywood sold as 3/4 in is usually 0.70-0.72 in, so a nominal 3/4 in bit cuts loose.

items.question: Which bits do I actually need to install a run of cabinets?
items.short_answer: A 35 mm hinge-cup bit, a 5 mm brad point for shelf pins, a 3 mm pilot bit and a flush-trim bit for filler strips cover a standard cabinet install.

items.question: How do I cut a hinge mortise in a door frame without chiselling for an hour?
items.short_answer: Rout the mortise with a straight bit against a template, then square the corners with a chisel. Set the depth to the leaf thickness plus 0.5 mm; too deep leaves the hinge hanging on its screws.

items.question: What hole saw size do I need for 1/2, 3/4 and 1 in conduit?
items.short_answer: Match the saw to the fitting: 7/8 in for 1/2 in EMT, 1-1/8 in for 3/4 in, 1-3/8 in for 1 in. Trade size describes the bore, not the hole.

items.question: Where am I allowed to drill through a floor joist?
items.short_answer: Holes go in the middle third of the joist depth, no bigger than one third of the depth, at least 50 mm from the top and bottom edges. Never notch the bottom edge.

items.question: What bit shapes a stair tread nosing?
items.short_answer: A 1/2 in radius round-over gives a standard tread nose; a bullnose bit fully rounds it. Above 25 mm diameter use a 1/2 in shank and slow the router to 12,000-16,000 rpm.

items.question: How do I cut a tongue and groove joint with a router?
items.short_answer: Cut the groove first at one third of the board thickness, then fit the tongue to it with 0.2 mm clearance. Groove first, tongue second, always.

items.question: Which small bits work for model making and wooden toys?
items.short_answer: Use brad-point bits of 2-6 mm for holes and 3 mm shank router bits for edges. Small bits snap under side load, so clamp the part and take passes no deeper than the bit diameter.

items.question: How do I get rust off drill bit shanks without ruining the flutes?
items.short_answer: Soak in a chelating rust remover or citric acid and scrub the shank with a brass brush. Keep abrasives off the flutes and replace any bit with a pitted cutting edge.

items.question: How do I strip paint off furniture without gouging the wood?
items.short_answer: Use chemical stripper and a card scraper. Do not sand softened paint or use a router or burr on painted wood, and test for lead paint before any abrasion or heat.

items.question: How do I repair a chipped edge on veneered board?
items.short_answer: Fill small chips with a wax or veneer sliver; rout a shallow rebate and inlay a strip when the chip is longer than 25 mm. Prevent them with a bearing-guided bit and a backer board.

items.question: The edge of my tabletop is chewed up — can I re-cut it straight?
items.short_answer: Re-cut the edge against a clamped straight edge with a flush-trim bit if you can lose 3-5 mm of width. For deep damage, rout past it and glue on a new solid edge band.

items.question: Can I run reclaimed lumber through a router or planer?
items.short_answer: Only after checking with a magnet and a metal detector. One hidden nail chips the carbide and the bit will not cut cleanly again without re-grinding.

items.question: How do I fix a screw hole that has wallowed out?
items.short_answer: Drill the hole clean to the next size up, glue in a hardwood dowel, and drill a fresh pilot. Glue and toothpicks do not hold a screw under load.

items.question: My tap and die set has surface rust — is it still usable?
items.short_answer: Surface rust on the body is cosmetic; rust, pitting or a chipped tooth on the cutting edge means retire the tap. Test a cleaned tap in aluminium before trusting it in steel.

items.question: How do I check whether my drill press table is square to the bit?
items.short_answer: Sweep a dial indicator around a 150 mm circle on the table; over 0.1 mm difference means shim the table. Without an indicator, use feeler gauges at four points against a rod in the chuck.

items.question: What is the most accurate way to measure the depth of a hole?
items.short_answer: Use a caliper depth rod at two points 90 degrees apart, referenced to the surface the bit registered on. Tape on the bit is a 0.5-1 mm guide, not a measurement.

items.question: How do I check that a drilled hole is actually the right size?
items.short_answer: Measure with caliper internal jaws at two points 90 degrees apart. A twist drill cuts 0.05-0.15 mm oversize, so a nominal 10 mm hole reads about 10.1 mm.

items.question: How do I check that a tap is cutting the thread I want?
items.short_answer: Run the matching bolt or a pitch gauge through the hole before assembly. A bolt that threads in by hand for its full length with no wobble passes; binding or wobble means the wrong drill or a worn tap.

items.question: Can a worn bit shank be the reason my chuck slips?
items.short_answer: Measure the shank with a micrometer at three points. A 1/4 in shank under 6.30 mm or more than 0.02 mm out of round will slip and should be replaced.

items.question: How do I measure the gap under a door before laying a new floor?
items.short_answer: Stack an offcut of the new flooring plus underlay under the door and add 3 mm for swing. Whatever the tightest point reads is the gap you need; doors are rarely parallel to the floor.

items.question: How do I know if my router table fence is straight and square?
items.short_answer: Cut a test piece and measure both ends: more than 0.2 mm taper over 200 mm means the fence is off. Or measure fence to bit at the infeed and outfeed edges and compare.

items.question: How do I make a router template that stays accurate over 50 parts?
items.short_answer: Cut the template from 6 mm MDF or 8 mm acrylic, file to the line, and use a top-bearing pattern bit. Measure the template with calipers rather than copying a finished part, because errors compound.

items.question: What is the fastest reliable way to drill 100 identical holes?
items.short_answer: Use the quill depth stop plus a fence and a hard stop on the table, and clamp each part instead of holding it. Repeatability comes from the stops, and the first part must be measured before the batch runs.

items.question: Can I drill a stack of parts at once instead of one at a time?
items.short_answer: Stack 2-5 parts under a template and clamp hard: workable in wood to about 30 mm total, and 2-3 plates in metal with cutting fluid. Two clamps, or the stack shifts between holes.

items.question: How do I hold small parts safely when routing?
items.short_answer: Hold small parts on a carrier board with stops, or with a handscrew, toggle clamps or carpet tape. Keep the fence opening as small as the cut allows so the bit cannot pull the part in.

items.question: Should I rotate bits through a long production run?
items.short_answer: Rotate bits every 50-100 parts and log which bit cut which batch. Rotation spreads wear and makes a failing edge show up as a change in sound before it ruins parts.

items.question: Is one large bit set better than several smaller sets?
items.short_answer: Buy several small sets when you know your size range; buy one large set when you need every size on hand. Steel grade and case quality matter more than piece count.

items.question: Should I rent a specialty bit or buy one I will use once?
items.short_answer: Buy when the bit costs less than about three rentals or you can name a second job for it. Rent when it needs a machine you do not own, and ask about tooling condition first.

items.question: Do I need spare pilot drills and arbors for my hole saws?
items.short_answer: Keep two spare pilot drills and one spare arbor per thread size. The pilot snaps long before the saw wears out, and a saw without a matching arbor cannot be used at all.

items.question: Should I buy tooling per project or stockpile a full range?
items.short_answer: Buy per project until you can name three future jobs for a size. Stock a full range only for trade work you repeat, or when a shopping trip costs you a day.

items.question: Is a 40-piece tap and die set worth it compared with buying singles?
items.short_answer: A 40-piece set wins when you work across M3 to M12, because singles plus a wrench and die stock cost more. For two sizes, buy good singles of the grade you need.
